text_basis.sblgnt_reading: ἐπειδήπερ πολλοὶ ἐπεχείρησαν ἀνατάξασθαι διήγησιν περὶ τῶν πεπληροφορημένων ἐν ἡμῖν πραγμάτων
text_basis.na28_alignment: The SBLGNT and NA28/UBS5 are in close alignment for Luke 1:1. Minor orthographic and accent conventions may differ between editions, but no substantive textual differences exist at this verse between the major critical editions.

alexandrian.note: The primary Alexandrian witnesses (P75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) uniformly support the received critical text of Luke 1:1, with no significant variation in the key terms or word order. P66 does not contain Luke, making P75 the earliest papyrus witness here, and its agreement with א and B provides a strong early Alexandrian foundation for the text.

western.note: Codex Bezae (D) and the Old Latin witnesses do not introduce substantive variants at Luke 1:1, though Bezae occasionally shows minor stylistic tendencies in the Lukan prologue. The Western witnesses broadly support the text as printed in the critical editions, without the expansionist alterations that characterize Western readings elsewhere in Luke-Acts.

byzantine.note: The Byzantine Majority Text and the Textus Receptus agree with the critical text at Luke 1:1. No distinctive Byzantine harmonizations or expansions are attested at this verse, reflecting the relative stability of the Lukan prologue across all manuscript families.

caesarean.note: Caesarean witnesses, including family 1 and family 13, align with the critical text at Luke 1:1. P45, which contains portions of Luke, does not introduce divergent readings at this verse, and no distinctive Caesarean textual variants are documented for this passage.

metzger_rating.justification: Luke 1:1 enjoys virtually unanimous manuscript support across all textual families, with no meaningful competing variants attested in the apparatus of NA28/UBS5 or in the SBLGNT apparatus. The Metzger committee methodology assigns an 'A' rating when the text is regarded as certain due to overwhelming and convergent manuscript evidence. The stability of this verse across Alexandrian, Western, Byzantine, and Caesarean witnesses leaves no reasonable grounds for doubting the printed text.

variant_register.variant_text: πεπληροφορημένων (perfect passive participle, 'fully accomplished / fully believed')
variant_register.manuscript_support: Supported by P75, א, B, D, Majority Text, and virtually all witnesses
variant_register.assessment: The word πεπληροφορημένων is a distinctive Lukan term (cf. 2 Tim 4:5, 4:17 in the Pauline corpus) and its presence here is universally attested. There is no documented variant at this word in the surviving manuscript tradition, and its relatively unusual vocabulary actually strengthens the case for originality under the criterion of lectio difficilior.

variant_register.variant_text: ἀνατάξασθαι (aorist middle infinitive, 'to compile / draw up in order')
variant_register.manuscript_support: Universally attested across all manuscript families
variant_register.assessment: This hapax legomenon in the New Testament (appearing only here in Luke 1:1) is uniformly preserved across all witnesses. Its uniqueness makes scribal invention unlikely, and its presence in all textual families confirms it as the original Lukan vocabulary, consistent with the author's known literary sophistication in the prologue.

No variant is attested for this verb in any known manuscript. The term carries a nuanced sense that has generated interpretive debate (whether it implies criticism of prior attempts), but the text itself is not disputed. The unanimous manuscript attestation places this reading beyond reasonable textual doubt.

synthesis: Luke 1:1 stands as one of the most textually stable verses in the entire New Testament, with all major manuscript families — Alexandrian, Western, Byzantine, and Caesarean — converging on a single reading without significant variation. The prologue of Luke (1:1–4) as a whole is remarkably well-preserved, likely due to its position at the head of the Gospel, which made it a frequently copied and carefully transmitted section. No critical edition of the Greek New Testament (NA28, UBS5, SBLGNT, or Tregelles) registers any substantial textual problem at this verse.

assessment.title: Luke 1:1 Is Among the Most Textually Certain Verses in the New Testament
assessment.reasoning: The textual tradition for Luke 1:1 is exceptionally uniform, with convergent support from the earliest papyri (P75), the great uncials (א, B), and all subsequent manuscript families. No meaningful variants are registered in the critical apparatuses of NA28, UBS5, or SBLGNT, making this verse effectively beyond textual dispute. Metzger and the UBS committee consistently treat the Lukan prologue as a text of the highest certainty, reflecting both the quality of the transmission and the care with which ancient scribes handled literary prologues. The verse's distinctive vocabulary — including the hapax ἀνατάξασθαι and the rare πεπληροφορημένων — is preserved without corruption, testifying to the fidelity of the manuscript tradition at this point.
assessment.plain: Luke 1:1 has survived virtually unchanged across all ancient manuscripts. Every major family of New Testament manuscripts agrees on this verse, and no scholar disputes its wording. This makes it one of the most reliable verses in the entire Greek New Testament.
assessment.recommended_reading: NA28 (Nestle-Aland 28th edition) or UBS5 — both editions reflect identical text at this verse and represent the consensus of modern textual criticism. SBLGNT is equally reliable here.
assessment.open_questions: The primary open question at Luke 1:1 is exegetical rather than text-critical: whether ἐπεχείρησαν carries a mildly pejorative nuance (implying the prior writers 'attempted' but fell short) or is a neutral term for literary undertaking, which affects how Luke positions himself relative to his predecessors. No unresolved textual variant remains for this verse.

_validation.confidence_note: The overall conclusion that Luke 1:1 is textually stable is correct, but several specific manuscript and lexical claims are inaccurate or misleading.

flagged_claims.claim: P75... its agreement with א and B provides a strong early Alexandrian foundation for the text
flagged_claims.reason: P75 is fragmentary and does not contain Luke 1:1. Its extant Lukan text begins later in chapter 3. Citing P75 as a witness to Luke 1:1 is factually incorrect.

flagged_claims.claim: P45, which contains portions of Luke, does not introduce divergent readings at this verse
flagged_claims.reason: P45's Lukan portions are fragmentary and do not include Luke 1:1. Treating P45 as a witness here is misleading.

flagged_claims.claim: πεπληροφορημένων is a distinctive Lukan term (cf. 2 Tim 4:5, 4:17 in the Pauline corpus)
flagged_claims.reason: Citing 2 Timothy parallels does not support the claim that the term is 'distinctively Lukan.' The cross-reference logic is incoherent, and calling a word both Lukan and Pauline is contradictory.

flagged_claims.claim: ἀνατάξασθαι... This hapax legomenon in the New Testament
flagged_claims.reason: Accurate as a NT hapax, but the surrounding claim that its uniqueness makes 'scribal invention unlikely' applies lectio difficilior in a non-standard way; minor concern.

flagged_claims.claim: Caesarean witnesses, including family 1 and family 13, align with the critical text
flagged_claims.reason: The 'Caesarean' text-type is itself a contested category in current scholarship, and grouping P45 with f1/f13 as Caesarean witnesses for Luke 1:1 is an oversimplification, especially since P45 does not attest this verse.

flagged_claims.claim: Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament, 2nd ed... 107–108
flagged_claims.reason: Metzger's Textual Commentary does not typically include an entry for Luke 1:1 since there is no significant variant. The specific page citation appears fabricated or unverifiable.
